query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A CoCrFeNi-based high‐entropy alloy whose composition is tailored by adding a minor fraction of aluminum will form a self-healing, protective alumina (Al2O3) layer during high‐temperature sliding in corrosive media, thereby exhibiting superior tribo‐corrosion degradation resistance compared with conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional equiatomic (or near-equiatomic) CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy without specific microstructural tailoring for oxidation protection.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by incorporating a minor amount (~5–10 at.%) of Al into the CoCrFeNi system using arc-melting synthesis followed by homogenization treatment to refine the microstructure.
generation.conditions: Exposing the alloy to elevated temperatures (300–600 °C) under sliding contact in a corrosive environment (e.g., a salt solution) that simulates extreme service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous and stable alumina (Al2O3) passivation layer and a refined microstructure that resists wear.
generation.mechanism: The added Al promotes the development of a protective oxide film during high-temperature exposure which minimizes the simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive attack (tribo-corrosion), resulting in slower degradation rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tailored HEA is expected to show lower wear and corrosion rates, which translates into enhanced durability under combined thermal and tribological stress compared to the conventional CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (wear rate, corrosion rate) measured on a conventional CoCrFeNi HEA or similarly used structural alloy under identical high-temperature, corrosive sliding conditions.
generation.boundary: This improved performance is anticipated under the specific conditions of 300–600 °C and corrosive salt environments; behavior in other temperature ranges or corrosive media may differ.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by known benefits of passive alumina formation, the exact optimal Al content, long-term stability of the passive film, and quantitative performance enhancement require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEAs: one consisting of a conventional CoCrFeNi alloy (control) and the other with an added ~7 at.% Al synthesized via arc-melting and homogenized to ensure microstructural uniformity. Subject both alloys to tribo-corrosion testing by performing sliding wear tests in a corrosive salt solution environment at temperatures ranging from 300 °C to 600 °C.
measurements: Wear rates (via profilometry or weight loss)
Corrosion rates (using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization)
Surface oxide composition and continuity (using XPS and SEM/EDS)
Microstructural analysis before and after testing (using TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-alloyed HEA does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in wear and corrosion rates compared to the conventional control alloy under identical test conditions, or if no continuous protective alumina layer is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To develop and design new alloy materials with lightweight and superior comprehensive performance. In this study, a MgAlTiVFeCo lightweight high-entropy alloy (LW-HEA) was fabricated via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS) to investigate the effects of sintering temperature on its phase structure, microstructure, densification, microhardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance, and corrosion resistance. The results indicate that the ball-milled MgAlTiVFeCo LW-HEA formed a simple solid solution phase with a BCC structure. After spark plasma sintering, the phase structure of the alloy changed, maintaining the BCC phase as the primary phase while accompanying the precipitation of secondary phases. When the sintering temperature reached 1000 °C, the alloy achieved a densification of 96.7% and a microhardness of 1235.5 HV. Its hardness value is comparable to the typical range of cemented carbides, demonstrating outstanding mechanical properties. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by experimentally identifying which HEA composition offers superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance.
